steps.title: SOFT PROMPTS GO HARD: STEERING VISUAL LAN-GUAGE MODELS WITH HIDDEN META-INSTRUCTIONS

conclusion: The paper’s central contribution is a method for constructing small image perturbations that act as cross‑modal soft prompts/meta‑instructions: given an image and a textual meta‑instruction, they optimize a perturbation so that a VLM’s answers both follow the meta‑instruction and remain grounded in the image, under a stealth constraint. Very closely related work already delivers this core capability. Bailey et al. (2023) (“Image Hijacks”) optimize pixel‑space images so that a VLM’s logits/outputs match those induced by target text prompts, explicitly showing that adversarial images can function as soft prompts controlling generative behavior. Bagdasarian et al. (2023), Qi et al. (2023), Shayegani et al. (2023), and “Multi‑Faceted Attack: Exposing Cross‑Model Vulnerabilities in Defense‑Equipped Vision‑Language Models” all craft constrained image perturbations that inject instructions via the vision pathway so that multimodal LLMs produce attacker‑specified, context‑appropriate outputs, often under visual‑similarity constraints. Relative to this body of work, the submission mainly contributes a more elaborate data/optimization pipeline (LLM‑synthesized QA pairs, evaluator filtering) and a particular empirical focus on benign “meta‑objectives” and semantic‑preservation metrics, which are secondary refinements rather than a new mechanism. Since the core technique—image perturbations as hidden cross‑modal prompts—is already well established, the paper’s novelty is not sufficient for a top‑tier venue.

core_judgments: The concept of providing meta-instructions through image inputs is not entirely novel—prior work, notably Bailey et al. (2023), has explored related prompt injection attacks via images.

The general algorithm employed, which involves creating a dataset of input-output pairs and training an image via projected gradient descent to maximize the likelihood over this dataset, closely aligns with the 'Behavior Matching' approach described by Bailey et al. (2023). As such, the methodological contribution is incremental rather than fundamentally new.

The novelty of this work lies less in the method itself and more in the scope, depth, and clarity of its empirical investigation, as well as the new insights it provides into the vulnerabilities of VLMs to image-based prompt injection.
